Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) — Overview

~40% of trauma deaths·~200,000 victims / year·50–80% caused by MVAs

Findings suggesting TBI: scalp wound, skull fracture, swelling/bruising, altered level of consciousness (LOC), nasal bleeding, or CSF rhinorrhea.

Other causes of LOC to keep on the differential
Spontaneous cerebral hemorrhage, drug overdose, metabolic derangement, alcohol intoxication.

TBI is a major neurosurgical problem with high mortality and heavy financial burden (acute care, rehabilitation, long-term recovery). Frequency is inversely related to severity — mild > moderate > severe — classified using the GCS.

Epidemiology:

Slide 4
  • TBI accounts for approximately 40% of all deaths.
  • About 52,000 US deaths per year result from TBI.
  • Annually, 200,000 victims of TBI need hospitalizat.
  • 1.74 million persons sustain mild TBI requiring an office visit or temporary disability for at least 1 day.
  • The financial cost is approximately $4 billion per year.
  • Leading cause of death and disability in trauma → head injury. 432 ×4

Scalp & Skull Injuries

Scalp Injury

Types: laceration, abrasion/friction injury, degloving injury. Subgaleal hematoma = hematoma beneath the scalp, outside the skull.

⚠ Do not underestimate scalp bleeding
The scalp is highly vascular — significant external blood loss can cause hypovolemic shock even without any internal (intracranial) bleeding.

Notes

Skull Fractures

Morphology: linear or depressed. A depressed fracture can compress the brain and raise ICP. Fractures may involve the cranial vault or the skull base, and may be:

Closed — scalp intact
Open — scalp lacerated, fracture exposed through the wound
Key rule of thumb
A skull fracture increases the likelihood of needing surgery at every TBI severity — even when the GCS is preserved.

Indications to Operate on a Depressed Skull Fracture

Depression greater than the thickness of the skull bone
Significant brain compression
CSF leakage through the wound
Open skull fracture
Conservative management
A linear fracture can generally be managed conservatively if the scalp is intact, the patient is neurologically normal, and the depression does not exceed skull thickness.

Basilar Skull Fracture

The skull base contains foramina transmitting cranial nerves and vessels — both may be injured; vascular imaging may

be required.

Fracture SiteClassic Clinical Sign
Anterior cranial fossaRaccoon eyes (periorbital ecchymosis)
Middle / temporal fossaBattle sign ± CSF otorrhea
Dural laceration at the temporal bone may cause CSF leak from the ear (CSF otorrhea). MASTERY CHECKLIST — SKULL & SCALP TRAUMA
1 Scalp bleeding alone can cause hypovolemic shock — never dismiss it.
2 Depressed fracture > bone thickness, open fracture, CSF leak, or significant compression → operate. 3
Anterior fossa → raccoon eyes; middle fossa → Battle sign / CSF otorrhea.
4 Any skull fracture raises surgical risk regardless of GCS.
A skull fracture raises the chance of needing surgery at every GCS.

Secondary Brain injury

Slide 18
  • Brain damage occuring after the initial trauma
  • Causes
  • Ongoing cellular damage, disrupted BBB and cerebral auto regulation
  • Secondary to brain edema, and brain herniation.
  • Intracranial hematoma.
  • Hypoxia.
  • Decreased CBF secondary to hypotension.
  • Ischemia & vasospasm.
  • CSF leak & Infection.
  • Hydrocephalus.
  • Secondary brain injury follows → hypoxia. 438 ×2

CauseEffect
Excitatory amino acids (EAAs), including glutamate and aspartate.cause cell swelling, vacuolization, and neuronal death.

Notes

Primary vs. Secondary Brain Injury

Primary Brain InjurySecondary Brain Injury
TimingAt the moment of impactDevelops over hours–days after trauma
Preventable?No — cannot be reversed or prevented once it occursYes — the major potentially preventable/treatable component
ExamplesDiffuse axonal injury, concussion, contusion The Secondary-Injury Vicious CycleBBB disruption, cerebral edema, hematoma/contusion enlargement (2–3 days), hypoxia, raised ICP, reduced perfusion → ischemia
↓ Cerebral blood flow / perfusion·Brain injury→Cerebral edema→Ischemia→→↑ ICP·↑ BBB disruption

...which drives further edema and ↑ ICP — the cycle repeats. Excitatory amino acids amplify swelling and neuronal death; metabolic disturbance alters consciousness.

Cerebral perfussion pressure (CPP)

Slide 21
  • CPP = mABP – ICP
  • Both should be monitored continously
  • CPP Should be ≥ 60–70 mmHg.
  • < 40mmHg -------- Disturbd autoregulation
  • < 30 mmHg -------- Brain infarction
  • Neurosurgical intervention specially against any increase in ICP.
Notes

Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP)

CPP = MAP − ICP
↑ ICP → ↓ CPP | ↓ MAP → ↓ CPP | ↑ MAP can compensate for raised ICP and preserve perfusion.
CPPSignificance
Target 60–70 mmHgGoal range in severe TBI management
< 40 mmHgCerebral autoregulation/perfusion becomes significantly impaired
< 30 mmHgIschemia/infarction cycle established
Brain Herniation & GCSSevere TBI requires continuous arterial-line BP/MAP monitoring, ICP monitoring, and continuously calculated CPP.
patterns simultaneously.Herniation or brain shift on CT is anatomical evidence of significantly raised ICP, even without direct ICP monitoring. Types: subfalcine, uncal, central, tonsillar, external. Large mass lesions (e.g., epidural hematoma) can cause multiple
⚠ Grave prognostic sign
GCS 3 + bilateral fixed, dilated pupils → extremely poor prognosis; suggests established herniation with brainstem infarction.

GCS is a reproducible, standardized language used to communicate level of consciousness — essential for TBI severity classification and prognosis. Higher GCS / following commands → generally better prognosis.

MASTERY CHECKLIST — INJURY PHYSIOLOGY
Primary injury = fixed at impact; secondary injury is the treatable target.
1
2 CPP = MAP − ICP; keep CPP 60–70 mmHg; below 30 mmHg, infarction is established. 3 Herniation on CT = raised ICP even without a monitor.
4 GCS 3 + fixed dilated pupils = brainstem herniation, dismal prognosis.
  • CPP = MAP − ICP 429 ×2 431 427 426; calculate it → 60 432; keep it above → keyed 75. 426
Uncal herniation → ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil (CN III) + contralateral hemiparesis. GCS 3 + bilateral fixed dilated pupils → dismal prognosis.

Chronic SDH

Slide 25
  • Minor Head trauma
  • Elderly patient
  • Delayed presentation
  • Bleeding from bridging veins
  • Headache, Dementia, confusion, personality changes, hemiparesis, or coma
  • Treated by burr holes
  • Usually good prognosis
  • Elderly on aspirin, fall 2–3 weeks ago, confusion and hemiparesis → chronic subdural haematoma 432 ×3 Gift 431
  • Stable assault victim with head injury → haemodynamic and neuro-vital monitoring 437; SDH with other injuries → advanced haemodynamic and neuro monitoring 436; unresponsive and snoring → jaw thrust. 432 ×3
Notes

Traumatic Intracranial Hemorrhage: EDH vs. SDH

Head-to-Head Comparison

Epidural Hematoma (EDH)Subdural Hematoma (SDH)
LocationOutside the duraBeneath the dura
CT shapeLens / biconvex-shapedCrescent-shaped
Suture relationRespects suturesDoes not respect sutures
Source of bleedingUsually arterial (skull-fracture associated)Usually venous — torn bridging veins
MechanismDirectly under a skull fractureAcceleration–deceleration injury
Underlying brain injuryUsually more localized, less diffuse injuryMore diffuse underlying brain injury
PrognosisBetter — dramatic improvement possible after evacuationWorse — injury often more significant than the hematoma alone
Classic finding — Lucid Interval (EDH)
Trauma → initial LOC → normal/recovered period for ~1–4 h → second deterioration/LOC. The initial LOC is the concussive effect; during the lucid period the hematoma keeps enlarging until mass effect/↑ICP causes deterioration. Lucid interval strongly suggests EDH → urgent imaging.
  • EDH bleeds from the middle meningeal artery 439 426; lucid interval = consciousness between two periods of unconsciousness 439 → epidural. 426
  • Lens-shaped → epidural 441 431; crescent-shaped → subdural 441 434 ×3 435 437; minor fall, alert then unconscious, crescent lesion → bridging veins. 442
Notes

Evolution of SDH on CT (High-Yield)

StageCT DensityDescription
AcuteHyperdenseWhite, fresh solid clot
SubacuteIsodenseSame density as brain — can be subtle
ChronicHypodenseLiquefied, "like water"

Chronic SDH Risk Factors & Presentation

Elderly patients
Antiplatelet / anticoagulant use
Cerebral atrophy → stretched bridging veins
Gradual enlargement over weeks–months
Headache
Focal weakness or numbness
SDH Management — matches the physical state of the clot
Acute (hyperdense, solid): cannot be drained through a small hole — significant hematoma requires craniotomy and evacuation.
Chronic (hypodense, liquefied): evacuated effectively with burr-hole drainage + drain.
History (recent trauma → acute; presentation after weeks → chronic) plus imaging distinguishes the two. Middle meningeal artery embolization is an evolving adjunct for chronic SDH.
MASTERY CHECKLIST — EDH VS SDH
Lens-shaped, respects sutures = EDH. Crescent-shaped, crosses sutures = SDH.
1
2 EDH = usually arterial + skull fracture; SDH = venous, bridging veins, acceleration–deceleration. 3 Lucid interval = EDH until proven otherwise — urgent imaging.
4 Acute SDH (white/solid) → craniotomy; chronic SDH (dark/liquid) → burr-hole drainage. 5
SDH generally carries a worse prognosis than EDH due to diffuse underlying injury.

  • Raised ICP treatment → head elevation 429 ×3 427; most potent and fastest way to lower ICP → controlled hyperventilation 437 ×3 — works by cerebral vasoconstriction 434 ×2; raised ICP with normal MAP over the coming days → mannitol. 426
Notes

Initial Management & Disposition

⚠ Always ATLS ABCDE first
Airway → Breathing → Circulation → then the remaining trauma survey. Do not prioritize ICP monitoring or hematoma management before ABC stabilization.

After stabilization: prevent secondary injury → determine BP/MAP → determine ICP when indicated → obtain imaging → look for fracture/EDH/SDH/other injury → decide definitive management.

Admit / Observe After Head Injury When:

Abnormal GCS / neurological status
Signs of skull fracture
Weakness, numbness, or seizures
Young children (unreliable assessment)
Alcohol/drug intoxication — observe until sober
No safe supervision after discharge

Indications for CT Brain After Head Injury

Change in LOC / GCS
Focal neurological deficit
Open skull fracture
CSF leak
Battle sign
Raccoon eyes

Skull X-ray is generally no longer used routinely in this setting.

ABCDE always comes first — before ICP or haematoma management.

Spontaneous Intracranial Hemorrhage

Spontaneous = intracranial hemorrhage without trauma.

Hemorrhagic tumor / bleeding into tumor

Anticoagulant therapy
Cerebral aneurysm (Marfan syndrome predisposes)
Hypertensive hemorrhage — basal ganglia, brainstem, cerebellum
AVM, arteriovenous fistula, cavernous malformation

Cerebral aneurysm

Slide 42
  • A cerebral aneurysm is an abnormal focal dilation of an artery in the brain that results from a weakening of the inner muscular layer (the intima) of a blood vessel wall. The vessel develops a “blister-like” dilation that can become thin and rupture without warning (SAH)
  • Types of aneurysms (morphology)
    • Berry (saccular)
    • Fusiform
  • Aetiology
    • Congenital
    • Injury (iatrogenic, trauma)
    • Infective (Mycotic aneurysm)

–

Notes

Cerebral Aneurysms — True vs. Pseudoaneurysm

Arterial wall, inner → outer: intima → media → adventitia.

True AneurysmPseudoaneurysm / Dissection
Wall layersAll 3 layers presentNot a true 3-layer dilatation
MechanismVessel wall dilatationIntimal injury → blood dissects into the wall
Causes another common site.— Morphology: saccular/berry or fusiform. Aneurysms preferentially arise at arterial bifurcations (higher shear stress) and rarely from the middle of a vessel segment. Anterior communicating artery = most common location; ICA bifurcation isTrauma, smoking, spontaneous injury, connective-tissue disease
MASTERY CHECKLIST — TRAUMATIC MANAGEMENT & ANEURYSM BASICS
1 ABCDE always precedes ICP/hematoma management.
2 Battle sign, raccoon eyes, CSF leak, or focal deficit → CT brain.
GCS at presentation is the single most important prognostic factor.
3
4 True aneurysm = all 3 wall layers; pseudoaneurysm = dissection through injured intima. 5 Anterior communicating artery is the most common aneurysm site.

Where Blood Collects — Intracranial Compartments

Epidural
Subdural
Subarachnoid

Intraventricular
Overall vs. atraumatic causes of SAH
Most common cause of SAH overall = trauma. Most common cause of atraumatic SAH = cerebral aneurysm. Aneurysm rupture may cause SAH alone or SAH + intracerebral hematoma.

Notes

Clinical Presentation of Aneurysmal SAH

Sudden, severe "worst headache of life" — thunderclap onset (0/10 → 10/10 within ~1 second)
Meningeal irritation: neck stiffness
May progress to ↓LOC from raised ICP, coma, or death
  • Cushing's triad: hypertension, bradycardia, slow/irregular breathing 435 432; early-morning headache of raised ICP → raised PCO₂ during sleep (vasodilation). 434 ×2
  • Meningitis signs with severe bilateral papilloedema → keyed mannitol (treat raised ICP; never LP first). 434 ×2
Notes

Grading Scales

WFNS GradeCriteriaPrognosis
1GCS 15, no motor deficitBest
2GCS 13–14, no motor deficitGood
3GCS 13–14 + neurological deficitIntermediate
4–5Progressively lower GCSProgressively worse
Based mainly on GCS ± motor deficit; lower WFNS grade = better prognosis.
Fisher GradeCT Findings
1No visible SAH / normal scan
2Thin SAH, blood thickness < 1 mm
3Thicker / more extensive SAH
4Associated IVH and/or ICH

Graded primarily by clot thickness; a Modified Fisher Scale also exists. Know the concept — detailed memorization was de-emphasized.

Imaging pathway in atraumatic SAH
Sudden severe headache → CT brain. If SAH is seen with no trauma history, suspect a vascular lesion (especially aneurysm) → next step is vascular imaging: CTA, MRA, or catheter angiography.

Notes

Complications of SAH

ComplicationKey Points
HydrocephalusBlood impairs CSF circulation/absorption
Cerebral vasospasmBlood around vessels triggers spasm → ↓CBF → delayed cerebral ischemia. Classic: patient improves after treatment, then develops new focal deficit (e.g., unilateral weakness) days later. Window: days 7–11 — close ICU monitoring even if initially normal.
RebleedingRuptured aneurysm can bleed again → secure the aneurysm as soon as possible; incompletely secured aneurysms retain risk.
Nimodipine — Level 1 evidence
Calcium-channel blocker given for 21 days in aneurysmal SAH to reduce the risk/consequences of vasospasm and delayed ischemia — one of the few Level 1 evidence treatments in neurosurgery.
Vasospasm peaks days 7–11 (new focal deficit after initial improvement) → nimodipine for 21 days (Level 1 evidence). Secure the aneurysm early to prevent rebleeding.

Treatment

Slide 54
Notes

Treatment of Cerebral Aneurysm

ApproachDetails
Microsurgical clippingCraniotomy/exposure → clip placed across the aneurysm neck
Endovascular — coiling / stentingCatheter-based occlusion of the aneurysm
Flow-diverting stentMesh device redirects flow through the normal lumen, away from the aneurysm — useful for fusiform aneurysms without a discrete neck
Endovascular treatment may be preferred when the patient cannot tolerate open surgery, or anatomy is unsuitable for clipping. Choice depends on aneurysm anatomy/pathology + patient condition.
MASTERY CHECKLIST — SAH
1 Thunderclap "worst headache of life" → CT brain → if no trauma, vascular imaging for aneurysm. 2 WFNS grades clinical severity (GCS ± deficit); Fisher grades CT clot burden.
Vasospasm peaks days 7–11 — watch for delayed focal deficits.
3
4 Nimodipine x21 days is the Level 1 evidence therapy for vasospasm.
5 Secure a ruptured aneurysm early — rebleeding risk persists until it is secured.

AVM

Slide 55
Notes

Arteriovenous Malformation (AVM)

Definition
Abnormal direct connection between arteries and veins without an intervening capillary bed. High-pressure arterial blood shunts directly into low-pressure veins → venous dilation and rupture risk.
Artery (high pressure)→Nidus (tangled vascular network)·Vein (dilated)

Rupture can occur from the nidus or the draining vein → intracranial hemorrhage / SAH.

Rupture risk
~2% per year. High-risk features (e.g., draining venous stenosis) increase risk. Ruptured AVM → treatment is indicated. Unruptured AVM: weigh natural rupture risk against treatment risk — not every incidental AVM needs treatment.

Presentations

Rupture / hemorrhage
Seizures / epilepsy
Steal phenomenon — blood shunted away from normal brain → ischemia → intermittent focal weakness/numbness (may itself be an indication for treatment)

Assessment: history of steal symptoms, prior rupture, or seizures; neuro exam; CT/MRI; vascular imaging/angiography

to show feeding artery, nidus, and enlarged draining vein (shunting can markedly enlarge veins such as the vein of Galen). During surgical disconnection, arterialized draining veins appear red and return to normal blue once shunting is eliminated.

Signs of Brain Injury
  • Lateralizing Signs (suggests brain herniation or stroke):
  • Unequal pupils → Brain herniation (midbrain compression)
  • Dilated, non-reactive pupil → Oculomotor nerve compression (CN III)
  • Weakness or paralysis on one side → Hemiparesis (stroke, brain
  • hemorrhage)
  • Spinal Cord Injury Signs:
  • Loss of sensation below injury level
  • Flaccid paralysis or spasticity
  • Loss of reflexes in lower limbs
If brain herniation is suspected, immediately administer:
  • Hypertonic saline (3% NaCl) or Mannitol
  • Elevate head of bed to 30°
  • Urgent neurosurgical consultation
Emergency Department (ED) Thoracotomy
A resuscitative thoracotomy is an extreme life-saving procedure performed in
patients with cardiac arrest due to penetrating trauma.
Indications for ED Thoracotomy:
  • Penetrating chest trauma with cardiac arrest
  • Blunt trauma with impending arrest
  • Signs of pericardial tamponade
  • Cardiac activity on ultrasound despite pulselessness
Procedure:
1. Perform a left anterolateral thoracotomy (4th-5th intercostal space)
